div.p: Although SMART NoC, as an emerging dynamically reconfigurable NoC architecture, is able to improve the communication efficiency significantly when scheduling real-time flows, it introduces uncertainty due to the nondeterministic latency. In this regard, we first study the schedulability of a set of arbitrary-deadline flows with given priorities. Based on schedulability analysis, an efficient priority assignment algorithm is proposed to minimize deadline misses. To our best knowledge, this is the first work of arbitrary-deadline flow scheduling on SMART NoC, which involves sophisticated computation of the worst case traversal time.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Recently, SMART [5] (Single-cycle Multi-hop Asynchronous Repeated Traversal ) NoC, a dynamically reconfigurable NoC, has been developed to significantly decrease the traversal time at running time by embedding asynchronous repeaters and adding bypass channels in traditional router, which can make a packet traverse the crossbar and link asynchronously for multiple hops in a single cycle and pave the path for real-time applications.

With this dynamically reconfigurable SMART NoC, the worst case traversal time is reduced, and the schedulability of real-time applications is also improved. The communication performance will be degraded, however, due to the contentions during transmitting. We need to arbitrate which flow can bypass the router, and which flows will be buffered at the router, thus introducing nondeterministic latency and prolonging the average traversal time. The communication issue was discussed on traditional NoC [1,2], and on SMART NoC [3].

In this paper, we take a first look at the problem of realtime flow scheduling on SMART NoC. We mainly target on the flows with arbitrary deadlines. That is to say, the deadlines of the flows are not restricted to be less than or equal to their periods. To check the schedulability of the flows transmitting on SMART NoC, we first predict the worst case traversal time of flows with given priorities under worst * Corresponding author: Weichen Liu.

div.head: PROBLEM DEFINITION
div.p: A real-time application consists of several cooperating tasks mapped on different IPs. Real-time packet flows are required between these tasks. In this paper, we give a non-trivial extension to the flows with arbitrary deadlines. Since the earlier packets may delay the later ones from the same flow, this scheduling problem is more difficult to solve, comparing with the flows that have constrained deadlines. Therefore, it's necessary to analyze the schedulability of an arbitrarydeadline flow fi specified as (Ci, Di, Ti, Pi).
Problem: For a set of periodic real-time flows with arbitrary deadlines transmitting on SMART NoC, the problem is to minimize the number of deadline misses.
To solve this problem, we should analyze the traversal time of a set of flows under worst cases, and assign corresponding priorities to guarantee timely delivery of packets.

div.head: TRAVERSAL TIME ANALYSIS OF FLOWS WITH GIVEN PRIORITIES
div.p: We define the concept of worst case traversal time of a flow under the worst scenarios, which is similar to worst case response time presented in real-time task scheduling on multicore systems. In general, this situation occurs when the packets of a certain flow are released simultaneously with all of the higher priority flows. But it is even worse when considering the upstream and downstream indirect interference [2,4,6], instead of simultaneous release of all flows.

During the transmission of an observed flow fi on SMART NoC, it may be preempted by higher priority flows due to contentions. This situation will make the observed flow buffered at the intermediate routers, where contention occurs, thus leading to additional wire and router delay Ai. If without contention, the packets from a flow will be transmitted to the destination in a single cycle. For any flow fi, the additional delay Ai is Ni × (Dw + Dr). Ni denotes the number of buffered times along the route, which can be calculated by using a certain algorithm. Dw and Dr refer to the wire delay and router delay, respectively.

For the arbitrary-deadline flows, allowing flows to have deadlines beyond their periods, the transmission of each packet may not be completed when the next packet is released, meaning that the earlier packets may delay the later ones from the same flow. In order to calculate the worst case traversal time of a packet from flow fi, we extend the busy period [7] to flow scheduling on SMART NoC in Fig. 1. During the priority-i busy period, all the flows of priority i or higher are transmitted throughout this time interval.

For the packets from flow fi, they may have the request to transmit simultaneously at a certain time during the busy period. Such packets from the same flow will be transmitted in order of releasing. The time length Ri(m) of the busy period is from the critical instant and ends until the completion of mth packet of flow fi, and is calculated by the following Eq. ( 1). The interference jitter J I j denotes the deviation between expected and actual release time and assumed to be Rj -Cj in [2]. As identified in [4], the authors add I down ji to Cj in their analysis, which is the additional interference due to the buffer space constraints.
div.formula: Ri(m) = (m + 1)Ci + Ai+ ∑ ∀f j ∈hp(f i ) ⌈ Ri(m) + J I j Tj ⌉ × (Cj + I down ji )(m = 0, 1, 2...).
div.p: (1) m = 0 means the first packet of flow fi, and the above equation will be terminated until Ri(m) ≤ (m + 1)Ti. The worst case traversal time is given by Ri = max(Ri(m) -mTi). If the condition Ri ≤ Di is met, the flow fi will be schedulable.

div.head: PRIORITY ASSIGNMENT
div.p: As discussed in previous section, we calculate the worst case traversal time Ri of a set of flows with given priorities. Based on the worst case traversal time, we find a proper priority ordering by using the following Algorithm 1.

The priority assignment is conducted starting from the lowest priority n, and each flow will be assigned a distinct priority. During the function UpperboundAnalysis, the upper bound of worst case traversal time Ri U B of each unassigned flow fi can be obtained when the indirect interference [2] is considered. The current priority p will be assigned to fi if Ri U B ≤ Di. If no flows meet this condition, the lower bound of worst case traversal time Ri LB is calculated when only considering the direct interference [2] and the additional buffered interference [4] in the function LowerboundAnalysis. Since Ri U B may be estimated too large, Ri LB is nearer to the actual traversal time. If Ri LB ≤ Di, the current priority will be assigned to this flow. Otherwise, the function Laxity-Analysis is called to calculate the slack time (the difference between deadline and Ci) of each unassigned flow fi and assign current priority to the flow that has the maximum slack time.

div.head: EXPERIMENT EVALUATION
div.p: In this section, we estimate the real-time performance of the proposed algorithm on SMART NoC, by comparing with rate monotonic scheduling and laxity monotonic scheduling. We use 2D-mesh based topology, and dimension order XYrouting. A large set of synthetic flows are conducted in our experiment. Fig. 2 describes the percentage of flows schedulable with different priority assignment in mesh size 10*10. It demonstrates averagely 66.8%, 57.9% performance improvement of the proposed algorithm comparing with other two algorithms.

div.head: CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we concentrate on scheduling a set of flows with arbitrary deadlines on SMART NoC. Although the bypass-forwarding feature can enhance the communication efficiency, it introduces the uncertainty due to the nondeterministic traversal time. To guarantee the overall schedulability of the whole SMART NoC, we first predict the worst case traversal time of flows with given priorities, and propose a priority assignment algorithm. Through our approach, the schedulability is improved significantly.
